title: FAO and Penn State launch Nuru, an offline phone app meant to confirm fall armyworm damage for African farmers
summary: Nuru, a machine-learning app from Penn State's PlantVillage and FAO, launched on 25 June 2018 to confirm fall armyworm damage offline on Android phones; no source reports an outcome for farmers.
account: On 25 June 2018 the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) announced from Rome that it and Pennsylvania State University had developed and launched Nuru, a talking app using machine learning. It runs offline on a standard Android phone. In FAO's description, a farmer holds the phone next to an infested plant and Nuru confirms whether fall armyworm caused the damage. FAO said that the pest first appeared in Africa in 2016 and spread across sub-Saharan Africa in 2017. It threatened the food security of more than 300 million people. Nuru was to complement FAO's Fall Armyworm Monitoring and Early Warning System (FAMEWS) app. Data validated by national focal points would flow into a global platform. The app was to add Swahili, French and Twi. PlantVillage wrote on 9 July 2018 that in Nuru's first two weeks it had tested the app with scientists in FAO field offices in Ethiopia, Zambia and Zimbabwe and with colleagues in Ghana and Burundi. Farmers in Kenya and Uganda had also used it. PlantVillage wrote that the beta app was underestimating fall armyworm damage, likely because of how the phone was held. Mongabay reported on 26 October 2018 that developers were still working on the fall armyworm version and that FAO planned to link it to FAMEWS by the end of 2018. The New York Times later reported that this fall armyworm tool served as the blueprint for the eLocust3m app of 2020. No source reports a test of the fall armyworm model's accuracy or an outcome for farmers. The published studies of Nuru's accuracy concern cassava.
purpose: Confirm fall armyworm damage on maize from a phone held next to the plant, offline, and feed reports into FAO's FAMEWS monitoring system.

provenance.basis: SHA-256 of the public record, its assessments, and its displayed answers and notes, excluding its own identifier and the derived coverage summary.

fields.account: On 25 June 2018 the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) announced from Rome that it and Pennsylvania State University had developed and launched Nuru, a talking app using machine learning. It runs offline on a standard Android phone. In FAO's description, a farmer holds the phone next to an infested plant and Nuru confirms whether fall armyworm caused the damage. FAO said that the pest first appeared in Africa in 2016 and spread across sub-Saharan Africa in 2017. It threatened the food security of more than 300 million people. Nuru was to complement FAO's Fall Armyworm Monitoring and Early Warning System (FAMEWS) app. Data validated by national focal points would flow into a global platform. The app was to add Swahili, French and Twi. PlantVillage wrote on 9 July 2018 that in Nuru's first two weeks it had tested the app with scientists in FAO field offices in Ethiopia, Zambia and Zimbabwe and with colleagues in Ghana and Burundi. Farmers in Kenya and Uganda had also used it. PlantVillage wrote that the beta app was underestimating fall armyworm damage, likely because of how the phone was held. Mongabay reported on 26 October 2018 that developers were still working on the fall armyworm version and that FAO planned to link it to FAMEWS by the end of 2018. The New York Times later reported that this fall armyworm tool served as the blueprint for the eLocust3m app of 2020. No source reports a test of the fall armyworm model's accuracy or an outcome for farmers. The published studies of Nuru's accuracy concern cassava.

produced_by: FAO-Penn State collaboration under FAO's five-year fall armyworm program launched October 2017
Android phones able to run the model offline
must_hold: Farmers hold the phone next to an infested plant
National focal points validate reports through FAMEWS

echoes.setting: eLocust3m locust app built by Penn State with FAO in under a month, reusing the fall armyworm app as blueprint
